This proposal specifies a mechanism for sending Zcash payments via any unmodified (secure) messaging service, printed medium, or other channel over which a short string can be conveyed. The sender need not know the recipient's address and the recipient need not have a Zcash wallet already installed.
A payment is created by deriving a fresh 32-byte

from that secret, and sending funds to its payment address, an Orchard-protocol address (funded in the Ironwood pool from NU6.3 activation onward). The payment secret, together with a block height from which the funds can be found and optional advisory metadata (amount and description), is encoded in the fragment of an ordinary HTTPS URL. Because the fragment is never sent to the server named by the URL, the host serves only as an
target for wallet software and as a landing page for recipients without a compatible wallet.

Anyone who learns the URI can claim the payment: their wallet derives the payment wallet, scans the chain from the given height, and sweeps every note it finds into an address of its own in a single transaction, taking the whole balance rather than the advertised amount. Until that happens the minter can take the funds back by the same procedure; there is no on-chain expiry and no limit on the age of a payment. A claim transaction is normally an ordinary fully-shielded transaction, indistinguishable on chain from any other, and it is constructed so that the payment secret does not grant visibility of where the funds went after the claim.

The proposal specifies the syntax and semantics of Payment-Encapsulating URIs, the derivation of payment wallets, the workflow of minting, claiming and reclaiming payments, and the behaviour expected of wallet software and of hosts that appear in payment URIs. It also describes, informatively, the payment-link formats already deployed by the Vizor wallet, which follow the same model of a bearer secret for a standard single-account wallet.

Alice wants to send a 1.23 ZEC payment to Bob. She doesn't have Bob's Zcash address — and Bob may not even have a wallet or have heard of Zcash! However, she does have some end-to-end encrypted channel to Bob on a secure messaging app, such as Signal or WhatsApp. She instructs her own Zcash wallet to send 1.23 ZEC on that channel. Her wallet derives a new payment secret from her wallet seed, sends 1.2301 ZEC to the corresponding payment address, and constructs a payment URI containing the payment secret, which she sends to Bob via the secure messaging app.
Bob receives the message, which looks as follows:
This message contains a Zcash payment. Click the following link to view it and receive the funds using your Zcash wallet app:
If you do not yet have a Zcash wallet app, see:
Bob clicks the link. His Zcash mobile wallet app (which is already installed and has configured itself as an

) shows up and tells Bob that a payment of about 1.23 ZEC awaits him. The wallet app scans the block chain from block 3400000 for the funds, confirms that they are present and unspent, and offers to claim the payment. Bob clicks the “Claim” button, and his wallet app generates a transaction moving the money to his own address (using the extra 0.0001 ZEC he has received to pay the transaction fee). When this transaction is confirmed on chain the payment is final, and Bob can send the funds to other parties.
If Bob had no compatible wallet installed, following the link would instead have shown him a static web page at
explaining what the link is and where to get a wallet; the page never learns the payment secret, which stays in the fragment on Bob's device.

The same mechanism serves "gift card" style uses: a merchant or event organiser mints a batch of payments, prints each URI as a QR code, and funds each card once. Whoever receives a card claims it; cards that are never claimed are reclaimed by the minter after an announced date.

This proposal enables sending of funds without exposing users to the notion of payment addresses and their secure distribution. Instead, funds can be sent using any pre-existing communication channel, by a single message sent unidirectionally from the sender to the recipient. This message conveys all the information needed to obtain control of the funds, compactly expressed as a textual URI.

Consequently, all functionality related to contact discovery and secure-channel establishment can be delegated to the message app(s) with which the user is already familiar, and in which the user has already established communication channels to many of their contacts.

Moreover, funds can be sent to users who have not yet installed wallet software and who do not yet have a payment address. The recipient can collect the funds at any later time by installing suitable software. This also makes the mechanism suitable for onboarding: a payment URI can be printed, handed out at an event, or embedded in a gift card, and the recipient's first interaction with Zcash can be receiving money rather than generating an address.

Finally, this avoids the fat-finger problem of sending funds to the wrong address. The user sends funds via a known contact on, e.g., WhatsApp, who they have a relationship with or at least can confirm the recipient's identity. Moreover, even once funds are sent via a URI, they can be recovered if the other party does not claim them.
The proposal is complementary to ZIP 321

A URI-Encapsulated Payment involves two on-chain transactions: a funding transaction from the minter to the payment address, and a claim transaction from the payment address to the claimant. Both are normally fully-shielded transactions and are not distinguishable on chain from other transactions in the same pool, except through timing correlation and the statistics of their numbers of actions.

The holder of a payment URI holds the payment wallet's full viewing key. They can therefore see the funding transaction(s) and the fact that the notes were spent. The claim transaction is specified so that its output is

decryptable with the payment wallet's outgoing viewing key; consequently a party who later obtains the URI (for example, from a chat backup or a discarded printed card) learns that the payment was claimed, but not the claimant's address or any other details of the claim output. The trade-off is that the claimant's own wallet is the only record of where the funds went.
The minter learns when (and that) a payment was claimed, because the notes it can view become spent. The
parameters are readable by anyone who sees the URI, including in retrospect.
The host named in a payment URI never receives the payment secret in an HTTP request, because it is carried in the fragment. However, any script served by that host

read the fragment, so the host operator (or anyone who can modify its content) is in a position to steal unclaimed funds if the landing page is not static. Wallet software that handles the URI through an
avoids any request to the host at all.
This proposal's specification of URI-Encapsulated Payments, and the intended protocols for using them, is meant to fulfill the following requirements:
The protocol must not require the sender of a payment to stay online until the recipient receives the URI (let alone claims the payment).
URIs should be short enough to render conveniently, to fit in a QR code of modest size, and to be compatible with length-limited messaging platforms.
It must not be feasible for someone who has not seen the URI (or has compromised a party who has) to collect the funds.

No server, indexer, or other third party should need to learn the payment secret, and claiming should be possible using only the ordinary light-client infrastructure that a shielded wallet already depends on.
The URIs and protocol should minimize the likelihood of inadvertent misuse, and in particular the risks discussed in

The protocol must not leak any information (sender identity, recipient identity, amount, description) to third parties, other than inevitable metadata about the existence of a transaction, the inevitable network communication around sending/receipt of transactions, whatever leakage is induced by the communication channel used to transmit the URI, and whatever is voluntarily shared by the parties.
The URIs should allow for future modifications and expansion of the format, without risk of ambiguous parsing.

The on-chain footprint of payments that use this mechanism should be indistinguishable from normal fully-shielded transactions (except, possibly, for the statistics of the number of shielded inputs and outputs).
A payment should remain claimable for as long as its funds are unspent, so that a payment that is printed, kept, or opened late does not silently become unclaimable.

Don't lose funds, even if wallets crash, or everything but the sending wallet master secret is lost. Payments minted by a wallet should be recoverable from that wallet's seed, and a payment URI on its own should be recoverable by any wallet that can restore a standard mnemonic phrase.
It is outside the scope of this proposal to establish a secure communication channel for transmission of URI-Encapsulated Payments, or to protect the parties' devices from security compromise.

Claiming the payment may involve significant wait times, on the scale of minutes, as the requisite on-chain transactions are generated, mined and confirmed, and as the claimant's wallet scans the chain from the given height. This proposal does not try to solve this (though it does try to avoid imposing significant additional delays, and it does address how the intermediate state is conveyed to the user).
A URI-Encapsulated Payment is not a long-term store of value and is not a substitute for a wallet backup. See
This proposal does not provide an on-chain expiry for unclaimed payments. Reclaiming is a wallet-side action of the minter.

Rationale for advisory attributes being lenient
The funds held by the payment wallet are authoritative, and

Rejecting a URI because one of them is malformed would make a funded payment unclaimable in conforming wallets because of a display-only field, which is the worse failure for a bearer instrument that may already be printed. The strict attributes, by contrast, determine which wallet is scanned and from where; guessing at them could hide funds or point the claimant at the wrong wallet.

Rationale for an Orchard-protocol payment address and an all-pool claim

The Orchard protocol is used because it is the current shielded protocol, with the best privacy properties and the cheapest proofs on mobile devices, and because a Unified Address with a single Orchard Receiver keeps the payment address short. The funding pool follows the current pool for that protocol: the
after it, when the consensus rules no longer let value enter the
. Funding the current pool also keeps the usual claim transaction free of cross-pool transfers, which would be visible on chain as changes in pool balances.

Sweeping everything the payment wallet holds costs the recipient no privacy: the payment wallet is single-use, its keys are already known to the minter and to every holder of the URI, the destination is a shielded receiver of the claimant, and the payment wallet's outgoing viewing key is not used. Leaving funds in a pool that the claimant does not scan would only strand them, or leave them for whichever other holder of the URI takes them. Some deployed payment links (see
) describe a payment address with both Orchard and Sapling receivers, so Sapling funds do occur in practice.
Rationale for deriving the payment wallet through a BIP 39 mnemonic
Deriving the ZIP 32 seed via a BIP 39 mnemonic rather than directly from

means that the payment wallet is an ordinary single-account wallet: any Zcash wallet that can restore a 24-word phrase can recover the funds of a payment URI, even if it has no support for this ZIP, by restoring the phrase and scanning from the birthday. This provides a recovery path independent of any particular software and lets a wallet "upgrade" a payment into a persistent wallet if it chooses. The cost is one PBKDF2 derivation of 2048 iterations, which is negligible.

The minter conveys the Payment-Encapsulating URI to the intended recipient, over some secure channel (e.g., an end-to-end encrypted messaging platform such as Signal, WhatsApp or Magic Wormhole; a QR code scanned in person; or a printed card handed over directly).

If transmitted via a human-readable medium, such as a messaging app, the Payment-Encapsulating URI MAY be accompanied by a contextual explanation that the URI encapsulates a payment, and a suggested action by the recipient to complete the process (see

When sent via a human-readable medium that consists of discrete messages, the message that contains the URI SHOULD NOT contain any payment-specific or manually-entered information outside the URI itself, since this information may not be visible to the recipient (see

From this point, and until the payment is claimed or reclaimed, from the minter's perspective the payment is “in progress”; it SHOULD be conveyed as such to the minter; and MUST NOT be conveyed as “claimed” or other phrasing that conveys successful completion.

The recipient's device renders the Payment-Encapsulating URI, or an indication of its arrival, along with the aforementioned contextual explanation (if any). The user has the option of “opening” the URI (i.e., by clicking it), which results in the device opening a Zcash wallet app, using the local platform's
mechanism, or, failing that, the landing page of the host.

A messaging app MAY recognize URI-Encapsulated Payments, and render them in a way that conveys their nature more clearly than raw URI strings. If the messaging medium consists of discrete messages, and a message contains one or more URI-Encapsulated Payments, then the messaging app MAY assume that all other content in that message is automatically generated and contains no payment-specific or manually-generated information, and thus may be discarded during rendering.

The wallet conveys to the user one of the following states:
: no unspent notes have been found yet, or the notes found do not yet have enough confirmations (see below). The wallet SHOULD keep scanning and re-evaluating.

: one or more unspent notes with sufficient confirmations have been found, and their total value exceeds the fee of the claim transaction. The wallet SHOULD present the user with an option to claim the payment (e.g., a “Claim” button) and SHOULD show the amount that will actually be received.

The funds held by the payment wallet (notes and transparent outputs) were received from outside the claimant's wallet, and are therefore untrusted TXOs in the sense of ZIP 315 for the claimant: the temporary wallet MUST NOT treat them as trusted. Whether they are spendable, and how their state is displayed, follow the wallet's ZIP 315 confirmation policy for untrusted TXOs. A minter reclaiming funds that it sent itself applies its ZIP 315 policy to them in the same way, according to whether it treats them as trusted.
The aforementioned conditions may change over time (e.g., the notes may be spent by someone else in the interim), so the status SHOULD be updated periodically while the payment is displayed.
Rationale for not limiting the age of a payment

A claim window, such as refusing any payment whose birthday is more than 100000 blocks (about 87 days) behind the tip, bounds the scanning work that a URI can demand. It would also turn a bearer gift into an expiring one: cards that are printed, kept in a drawer, or opened after a holiday would become unclaimable in conforming wallets while their funds are still on chain, and falling back to restoring the mnemonic sentence in a general-purpose wallet is not something most recipients can be expected to do. The scanning cost of an old payment is the same as that of restoring any wallet with an old birthday, for a single account, and the user can be warned and can cancel. A hostile URI can therefore cost the user time but cannot take control of the scan.

This ZIP sets no confirmation numbers of its own; the classification of funds as trusted or untrusted is what matters, and ZIP 315 supplies the policy. It has been argued that a single confirmation suffices for the funding notes, because they were created expressly for a single-use wallet and so the usual concerns about untrusted senders do not apply. Provenance is not the risk, however: the minter still holds the payment secret (and, for seed-derived secrets, can always re-derive it), as may other parties who have seen the URI. If a chain reorganization removes the funding transaction or the claim transaction, the minter can double-spend the funding transaction's inputs, or another holder of the URI can have their own claim mined instead, and the claimant's apparent receipt disappears. These are exactly the risks that the ZIP 315 policy for untrusted TXOs addresses. The claim transaction itself is different: it is created on the claimant's device, so its output is trusted (see
When the user chooses to claim the payment, the wallet app constructs a single

It spends all funds of the payment wallet that satisfy the confirmation policy above: every unspent Orchard, Ironwood and Sapling note, and every unspent transparent output. The claim MUST sweep all of them. Where ZIP 317 fees, transaction size or the rules of a pool make a single transaction impractical, the wallet MAY claim in more than one transaction, each with the properties listed here.

It has exactly one non-dummy output, to a shielded receiver belonging to the claimant's own wallet, and MUST NOT send to a transparent receiver. Before NU6.3 activation the wallet SHOULD send to its Orchard receiver in the
; from NU6.3 activation onward it MUST send to an Orchard-protocol receiver in the
. Orchard-pool notes of the payment wallet are spent as ZIP 326 requires after NU6.3 activation (with fabricated same-address outputs
The output value is the sum of the inputs minus the transaction fee, so that the claim transfers the payment wallet's full spendable balance. The wallet MUST NOT limit the claim to the value of

The claim transaction MUST NOT use the payment wallet's outgoing viewing key, or any other key derived from the payment secret, to encrypt any of its outputs. The wallet MUST instead use the "no outgoing viewing key" construction of the protocol

The memo of the output SHOULD identify the origin of the funds as a URI-Encapsulated Payment, and MAY include the
value, truncated so that the memo does not exceed 512 bytes of UTF-8 and remains a valid text memo.
It uses the wallet's default transaction expiry (see ZIP 203

Before broadcasting, the wallet MUST show the user that funds are about to be claimed from a URI-Encapsulated Payment, the amount that will be received, and the destination account, and MUST allow the user to cancel. A wallet MUST NOT claim a payment without an explicit user action.

Once the claim transaction has been broadcast, the wallet MUST delete the temporary wallet, including its database and all key material derived from the payment secret, so that the payment wallet's keys are not retained on the device. The wallet SHOULD retain the payment URI itself (not the derived keys) until the claim transaction is mined, so that the claim can be retried if the transaction expires unmined, and SHOULD delete it afterwards.

The claimant's wallet SHOULD convey the payment status as “Claiming…” from the time that the user initiates the claim until the claim transaction is mined, and as “Claimed” once it is mined with the number of confirmations the wallet considers final. The claimed funds appear in the claimant's wallet as an ordinary received note.
Rationale for sweeping transparent and Sapling funds

Spending a transparent output, or moving value between shielded pools, is normally avoided because it is visible on chain. Here it reveals nothing about the claimant: the payment wallet is single-use, its keys are already known to the minter and to every holder of the URI, and the destination is still a shielded receiver of the claimant with no outgoing viewing key of the payment wallet. Leaving the value behind would strand it, or leave it for whichever other holder of the URI takes it.
Rationale for sweeping the full balance
Sending exactly the advertised amount would make

binding and would fail in two ways. Any excess (from over-funding, a top-up, or a fee reserve larger than the actual fee) would stay in the payment wallet, where anyone else who holds the URI, including the minter, could take it. And any shortfall (from a lower funding amount, or a fee higher than the reserve) would make the payment unclaimable until the minter topped it up. Sweeping the whole balance gives the claimant everything the URI controls, and the wallet shows the amount actually found before the user confirms.

The claim transaction is constructed on the claimant's own device, by the same wallet application that receives its output. The claimant's wallet SHOULD therefore record the claim transaction as soon as it is broadcast (so that the incoming funds are shown without waiting for it to be mined) and SHOULD treat it as a trusted transaction in the sense of ZIP 315

, so that its output's spendability and display follow the wallet's ZIP 315 confirmation policy for trusted TXOs. This is the "mark specific external transactions as trusted" allowance of ZIP 315: although the output is not an output of a transaction created by the claimant's wallet, its origin is known to be the payment wallet that the claimant's own device just controlled.
If the claim transaction expires unmined, or is otherwise rendered irrevocably invalid (e.g., by a reorganization), the wallet SHOULD convey this and SHOULD revert to the
Rationale for discarding the outgoing viewing key

A payment URI is frequently retained after it is used: in a chat history, a device backup, a printed card that is thrown away, or a screenshot. Everyone who later obtains it holds the payment wallet's full viewing key. If the claim transaction's output were encrypted to the payment wallet's outgoing viewing key, as a wallet normally does for its own spends, every such party could decrypt the output and learn the claimant's address and the amount they received. This includes the minter, who can re-derive a seed-derived payment secret at any time and would otherwise learn the claimant's address and be able to link later payments to it. Using a random

instead makes the claim output opaque to the payment secret. The trade-off is that the claimant cannot use the payment secret to prove or recover where the funds went; their own wallet is the only record, which is the same situation as for any other received note.

At any time prior to the payment being claimed, the minter is capable of cancelling the payment, by themselves claiming the payment into their own wallet (thereby “clawing back” the funds). The minter's wallet SHOULD offer this feature. A reclaim is a claim transaction as specified in
, constructed by the minter's wallet with one of its own shielded receivers as the destination; all requirements of that section apply, with confirmations as described in

There is no on-chain expiry: an unclaimed payment remains claimable, by the minter and by any holder of the URI, indefinitely. A minter who intends to reclaim unclaimed payments SHOULD announce the date after which it will do so, in the

Reclaiming is subject to a race: the minter and a holder of the URI can both construct claim transactions spending the same notes, and whichever is mined first succeeds. A wallet MUST treat the failure of its own claim transaction because the notes were spent elsewhere as a normal outcome and convey it as
(by someone else) rather than as an error.
If the minter's wallet has not yet broadcast the funding transaction, the payment can also be cancelled by discarding that transaction.
Reclaiming requires the minter to know the payment secret. If the minter has lost this state, it can be recovered deterministically for seed-derived payments (see

Wallet apps SHOULD let the user view the status of all payments they have minted, as well as all inbound payments (i.e., URI-Encapsulated Payments that have been opened in the app). The status includes the available metadata, and the payment's current state. When pertinent, the wallet app SHOULD offer the ability to claim any
inbound payment, and MAY offer the ability to reclaim any outbound payment that has not been claimed.
The minter's wallet can track the state of a payment it minted by scanning with the payment wallet's full viewing key: the payment is
while its notes are unspent and
once they are spent by a transaction that the minter's wallet did not create.

Wallet apps SHOULD actively alert the user (e.g., via status notifications) if a payment that they minted has not been claimed within a reasonable time period (e.g., 1 week), and offer to reclaim the payment.
Because seed-derived payment secrets are a deterministic function of the wallet seed, a minter that has lost all other state can recover its unclaimed payments.
The RECOMMENDED approach is for the minting wallet to persist, in storage that is backed up alongside the seed (for example wallet metadata encrypted under ZIP 325
and, for each minted payment, its
. Recovery then consists of re-deriving each payment wallet and scanning it from its recorded height.
If no such metadata is available, the wallet MAY fall back to a gap-limit search, similar to the “address gap limit” in BIP 44: derive the payment wallets for
, scan each from the minting wallet's own birthday, and stop after
consecutive indices whose payment address has never received a note. We specify a standard gap limit of
. Because each index is a separate full viewing key, this search costs one full scan per index; it is a fallback, not the primary mechanism.
A minter that uses random secrets has no such recovery path and MUST keep its own durable record of secrets if it intends to reclaim.

A claimant needs no recovery mechanism beyond the URI itself: a payment URI can be re-opened at any time until it is claimed, and the payment wallet can also be restored, by any wallet, from the 24-word mnemonic sentence that encodes the payment secret (see
This section is informative. It describes deployed formats; it is not part of the specification.

Kris Nuttycombe's draft "Mnemonic-Encapsulated Payment Links" describes that protocol; the shapes below are taken from it and from links observed in use.

The deployed protocol differs from this specification in its claim behaviour: it sweeps exactly the advertised amount, spends funds with a single confirmation instead of following ZIP 315, refuses links whose birthday is more than 100000 blocks behind the tip, and allows a Sapling destination. This specification does not adopt these choices; see
Rationale for sweeping the full balance
Rationale for not limiting the age of a payment
. Funds that a minter using these forms sent to a Sapling receiver are found and swept like any other funds of the payment wallet.
Anyone who learns a Payment-Encapsulating URI may take the encapsulated funds. The URI is a

. It should be sent over a secure channel and kept secret from anyone but the intended recipient. Common ways to leak it include: chat and device backups, screenshots, clipboard history, browser history and HTTP referrers (if the URI is ever opened in a browser), server and proxy logs (if it is ever placed in a query string instead of the fragment), notification previews, and printed copies.
The Payment-Encapsulating URI is like a magic spell that will teleport the money to the first person that clicks it and then does "claim".

The host named in the URI never receives the fragment in an HTTP request, but any JavaScript that the host serves can read it. Host operators should serve a static landing page with no analytics or third-party scripts, and wallets should handle URIs through applinks so that no request to the host is made (see
). Compromise of the host, or of a CDN or tag manager it embeds, would otherwise allow theft of every unclaimed payment opened in a browser.

URI-Encapsulated Payments may be captured by malicious local apps on the sender or receiver's platform, e.g., by screen capturing or clipboard eavesdropping. Wallet apps should use the platform's interaction and communication facilities in a way that minimizes these risks (e.g., use the “Share” API rather than a clipboard that is visible to all apps).

Likewise, if the URI is transferred by presenting and optically scanning a QR code, anyone who observes this QR code may be able to claim the payment and thus take ownership of the funds before the intended recipient. For example, an attacker may use a telephoto lens aimed at a point-of-sale terminal to steal QR-encoded payments sent to that terminal.

Printed payments ("gift cards") should be funded only once, while the printed medium is still in the minter's custody, and should be handed over in a way that the printed URI cannot be read beforehand (e.g., under a scratch-off layer or inside sealed packaging). A card that has been out of the minter's custody should never be topped up, since its secret may already have been copied.
parameter must not be greater than the height at which the funding transaction was mined; otherwise a claimant scanning from

will never find the funds and will report the payment as empty, even though the minter's wallet shows it as funded. Producers that generate the URI before the funding transaction is mined must use a height at or below the current chain tip, and a reorganization between URI generation and mining cannot move the funding transaction below that height.

Claim transactions discard the payment wallet's outgoing viewing key. This protects the claimant from everyone who later obtains the URI, at the cost that the claim output cannot be recovered from the payment secret (see
Rationale for discarding the outgoing viewing key
). Wallets must not "helpfully" encrypt the output to the payment wallet's outgoing viewing key for the sake of history display.

The temporary wallet used to scan and claim must be isolated from the user's own accounts and deleted after the claim is broadcast. Importing the payment wallet's keys into the user's main wallet would make a bearer secret, known to at least one other party, part of the user's own spending authority, and would cause the user's wallet to display and potentially reuse an address that others control.

Wallet UX must make clear that the funds come from a URI-Encapsulated Payment and let the user cancel before anything is broadcast. Opening a URI must not by itself move funds: an applink can be triggered by any web page, and a hostile page could otherwise cause a user to sweep a payment into their own wallet as a way of making them a party to a transfer they did not intend.
The claim memo may include the
text, which is attacker-controlled. Wallets must sanitize it (see
), truncate it to the memo size, must not interpret it as markup or as a URI, and should display it as the claim made by the URI's author.
Any web page can deliver payment URIs to a wallet through an applink. The intake bounds in
limit the work such a page can cause, and the temporary wallet is the only state a hostile URI can populate. A URI with a very old
can make a scan long; wallets warn about this and let the user cancel, rather than refusing old payments.

A claim sweeps every pool the payment wallet holds funds in. Sweeping transparent outputs, or Sapling notes into Orchard, reveals on chain the value that leaves the transparent or Sapling pool, but nothing about the claimant beyond that. Minters should fund the payment address in the current pool for the Orchard protocol (the
after it) so that the usual claim stays within one pool.

Users may have casually-established communication channels (e.g., they have entered the phone number of a new contact without bothering to double-check it), but may later mistakenly consider these to be adequately-authenticated secure channels for the purpose of sending a Payment-Encapsulating URI. Wallet apps should mitigate this where feasible, e.g., by indicating that the chosen messaging channel is previously-unused and thus should be more carefully checked.

Users may incorrectly believe that the payment has been irrevocably received even though they have not claimed it, or even though the claim has failed. Wallet software should correctly convey the status and set expectations, as discussed above.
Payment recipients may not notice the incoming payment notification and act on it (i.e., claim it) in a timely fashion. By the time they see it, the payment may have been reclaimed by the minter.
Users may not understand that URI-Encapsulated Payments are for one-time use, and attempt to use the same URI for multiple people or payments, resulting in race conditions on who receives the funds.
Users may confuse URI-Encapsulated Payments (as specified in the current ZIP) with Payment Request URIs of the form

. Normally these serve different workflows, and work in opposing directions (send vs. receive of funds), and thus ought to not arise in ambiguous context. Wallet apps should take care to not create or send a Payment-Encapsulating URI (which is for
funds) in a context where the user may be intending to

Users may attempt to use a Payment-Encapsulating URI as a “cold wallet”, e.g., by writing the URI on paper and putting it in a safe. This is dangerous. The payment secret is known to the minting wallet at the time when the URI is produced, and can be re-derived from the minting wallet's seed at any later time. Thus, an adversary who compromises the minting wallet may drain the "cold wallet".

The act and timing of claiming a payment is visible to the minter, which may be a privacy leak. Likewise, the timing of the funding transaction can be linked to the later claim, which may be a privacy leak.

The payment amount is readily visible to anyone who observes the Payment-Encapsulating URI, even in retrospect after the payment has already been claimed (e.g., if their device or chat log backups are later compromised). This may be a privacy concern, and in particular may put recipients of large payments at risk of undesired attention. Minters MAY omit

Usage of URI-Encapsulated Payments may train users to, generally, click on other types of URI/URL links sent in other messaging contexts. Malicious links sent via unauthenticated messaging channels (e.g., emails and SMS texts) are a common attack vector, used for exploiting vulnerabilities in the apps triggered to handle these links. Even though the fault for vulnerabilities lies with those other apps, and even though this ZIP uses deep link URIs in the way intended, there are none the less these negative externalities to encouraging such use.
was chosen to allow automatic triggering of wallet software on mobile devices, using the platform's

mechanism, while keeping the payment secret off the network: the contents of the fragment identifier are specified by HTTP as being resolved locally, rather than sent over the network. Any HTTPS host can be used, which lets each wallet vendor or service operate its own applink domain and landing page without a central authority, at the cost that the security of the landing page is the responsibility of each host operator (see
A reserved origin that does not resolve (for example a reserved domain with an invalid port number such as

), so that following the link without a wallet installed performs no network request at all. This gives defense in depth against a compromised landing page, but it requires a single party to control the domain and the applink whitelist for every wallet, produces a confusing error or blank page for users without a wallet, and in practice was found to be rejected or rewritten by some messaging platforms. The present design instead requires landing pages to be static and lets wallets avoid the host entirely.
: a custom URI scheme. This still allows for triggering application action (e.g., using Mobile Deep Links). However, on most platforms,

app installed on the device is able to register to handle links from (almost) any custom URI scheme. If the request is received by a rogue party, then the funds could be stolen. Also, custom URI schemes are not linkified when displayed in some messaging apps, and provide no fallback for users without a wallet.
scheme is already used to specify Zcash addresses and payment requests in ZIP 321
URIs of BIP 21, and is therefore unsuitable in any case.

Adding a confirmation code outside the URI that needs to be manually entered by the user into the wallet app, so that merely intercepting the URI link would not suffice. This does not seem to significantly reduce risk in the scenarios considered, and so was deemed to not justify the reduced usability.

The payment secret is Bech32m-encoded, rather than base64url or hex, so that it carries a checksum (a mistyped or truncated secret is detected rather than yielding an empty wallet), so that its Human-Readable Part identifies both the nature of the string and the network, and so that it survives case-normalization and is QR-friendly in the same way as Zcash addresses.
Rationale for scanning from a birthday

The recipient's wallet needs to find the notes related to the payment in order to verify their validity and then spend them. Earlier drafts of this ZIP considered several ways to identify those notes without scanning: listing note commitments in the URI, placing a public tag in the memo or in an extra output, or deriving a single note deterministically from the secret and the amount so that its commitment could be looked up in an index. All of these either lengthen the URI, leak information on chain, require infrastructure that light clients do not otherwise have, or constrain the funding transaction to a single note of a fixed amount.

The present design instead includes a birthday height in the URI and scans from there, which is exactly the operation a light client already performs for its own accounts and requires no additional infrastructure. Because the payment wallet is a single account with a known birthday that is usually close to the chain tip, the scan is short in practice. It also means that the payment address can be funded with any number of notes, at any time after minting, and that top-ups and partial reclaims behave naturally.

parameters are provided within the URI so that the metadata is available for presentation to the user before the chain has been scanned. They are advisory rather than binding because the on-chain state is the only thing a claimant can rely on, and because binding them would require either a note-derivation scheme (see above) or a signature over the URI by a key that the claimant has no reason to trust.

We do not include the sender's or receiver's identity in the URI, because the minting wallet may not know the name of who it is sending to (or even from). Moreover there is the risk that fraudulent sender/recipient information could be used. If necessitated by circumstances, claimed sender and recipient identity can be included in the

An on-chain expiry would require either a time-locked spending condition, which shielded Zcash does not provide, or a pre-signed reclaim transaction with a future expiry, which would have to be refreshed and would reveal the minter's intent on chain. Leaving reclaim entirely to the minter's wallet keeps the on-chain footprint ordinary and lets minters choose their own policy; the cost is a race that both parties must handle gracefully.
